people.b: Formed from the dust of the ground and given the breath of life; keeper of the garden, namer of the animals, and with Eve the first to disobey. Paul calls Christ 'the last Adam'.

people.role: The mother of all the living
people.b: Made from Adam's side, deceived by the serpent, and mother of Cain, Abel and Seth. Her name in Hebrew means 'life'. Christian tradition set Mary beside her as the 'new Eve'.
'A just and perfect man in his generations' who walked with God, built the ark, and received the covenant of the rainbow. Also the first to plant a vineyard.

Called out of Ur to a land he had never seen, promised descendants as many as the stars while childless, and asked to sacrifice the son he finally received. Jews, Christians and Muslims all count him as father.
Beautiful enough to endanger her husband in two royal courts, barren until ninety, and laughing behind the tent door when told she would bear a son — whom she named Isaac, 'he laughs'.
Bound on Moria, married to Rebecca from his father's country, deceived in his blindness by Jacob. The quietest of the patriarchs; the wells he re-dug are his story.
Chosen at a well for watering a stranger's camels; mother of twins who fought in her womb; the strategist behind Jacob's stolen blessing.
Heel-grabber, deceiver, dreamer of the ladder at Bethel, wrestler at the Jabbok who limped away with a new name. His twelve sons became the tribes of Israel.
Sold by his brothers, falsely imprisoned, raised to Pharaoh's right hand for reading dreams — and forgiving the brothers who sold him: 'you thought evil against me, but God turned it into good'.

Drawn from the Nile, raised in Pharaoh's house, called at the burning bush, he led Israel through the sea to Sinai and forty years in the desert, saw the promised land from Nebo, and died without entering it. God spoke with him 'face to face'.
Moses' brother and spokesman, maker of the golden calf, and yet the first high priest, whose rod budded and whose line held the priesthood.
Watched the basket in the reeds, led the women in song at the sea, and was struck with leprosy for speaking against her brother.
Moses' aide and one of two faithful spies; he led Israel across the Jordan, around Jericho, and to the covenant renewal at Sichem. His name is the Hebrew form of 'Jesus'.
Judged Israel under a palm tree and summoned Barac to war against Sisara; her victory song is among the oldest poems in the Bible.
Threshing wheat in a winepress when the angel called him 'mighty man of valour'; he tested God with a fleece and beat Madian with three hundred men, torches and jars.
A Nazirite from birth who killed a lion with his hands and a thousand Philistines with a jawbone, betrayed by Dalila, blinded, and victorious in death.
'Whithersoever thou shalt go, I will go.' A foreign widow whose loyalty to her mother-in-law led her to glean in the field of Booz and into the family tree of David and of Jesus.
Dedicated to the sanctuary by his mother Anna, called by name in the night as a boy, he anointed Israel's first two kings and warned what kings would cost.
Head and shoulders taller than anyone, chosen while looking for lost donkeys; a brave soldier undone by disobedience, jealousy of David, and despair. He died on Mount Gelboe.

Shepherd, harpist, giant-killer, outlaw, king of Judah and then all Israel, conqueror of Jerusalem, adulterer and penitent, father of a rebellious son. The Psalms carry his name and the Messiah his title, 'son of David'.
Heir to the throne who loved the man who would take it 'as his own soul', and died beside his father on Gelboe.

people.role: Wife of David, mother of Solomon
people.b: Seen bathing from the palace roof; her husband Urias was sent to die. Her second son was Solomon, and she secured his succession. Matthew names her in Jesus' genealogy only as 'the wife of Urias'.
Brought David the promise of an everlasting house, and later the parable of the poor man's lamb — 'thou art the man'.

Asked God for wisdom and received wealth and fame as well; built the Temple; wrote, by tradition, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song. His seven hundred wives turned his heart, and the kingdom split at his death.

Appeared from nowhere to announce a drought, fed by ravens, fed by a widow, victor on Carmel, fugitive on Horeb hearing a still small voice, carried to heaven in a chariot of fire. Expected to return before the Messiah.
Ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elias threw his mantle over him; asked for a double portion of his spirit; healed Naaman, multiplied oil and bread, raised the Sunamite's son.
Reformer king who cut the tunnel that still carries water under Jerusalem, held out against Sennacherib's siege, and was granted fifteen more years of life when the sun's shadow went back.
King at eight; at twenty-six the book of the Law was found in the Temple and he tore his garments and purged the land of idols. Killed at Mageddo fighting Pharaoh Nechao.

Saw the Lord enthroned in the Temple the year King Ozias died; counselled kings through the Assyrian crisis; the book bearing his name — sixty-six chapters over two centuries — is the prophet most quoted in the New Testament. Tradition says he was sawn in two.
Called as a boy, forbidden to marry, thrown into a cistern, he watched the city he warned burn and was dragged to Egypt. Promised a new covenant written on the heart.
A priest deported to Babylon who saw God's chariot beside a canal, acted out the siege of Jerusalem, and prophesied to a valley of dry bones.

people.role: Seer at the court of Babylon
people.b: Deported as a youth, he refused the king's food, interpreted Nabuchodonosor's dreams and the writing on the wall, survived the lions, and saw one like a son of man coming on the clouds.
A Jewish orphan who became queen of Persia and risked her life — 'if I perish, I perish' — to save her people from Aman. The feast of Purim remembers her.
Priest and scribe who led a return from Babylon and read the Law aloud to the people from dawn to noon. Jewish tradition credits him with fixing the text of the Torah.
Cupbearer to the Persian king who wept at the news of Jerusalem's broken walls, got leave to rebuild them, and did it in fifty-two days with a sword in one hand and a trowel in the other.
A man of Hus who lost everything in a day, sat in ashes, argued with his comforters and with God, and was answered out of the whirlwind.
Fled from God by ship, swallowed by a great fish, preached to Nineveh and sulked when it repented. Jesus offered his three days as the only sign.
A widow who entered the Assyrian camp, beheaded Holofernes with his own sword, and returned with his head in a bag.
Buried the dead at risk of his life, was blinded by sparrow droppings, and was healed by his son with the guidance of the angel Raphael.
'The Hammer'. Led the guerrilla war against Antiochus, cleansed and rededicated the Temple (Hanukkah), and died in battle.
A girl of Nazareth who said 'Be it done to me according to thy word'; sang the Magnificat; pondered in her heart; asked for wine at Cana; stood at the cross; prayed with the apostles at Pentecost.
A carpenter, 'a just man', who obeyed four dreams and never speaks a recorded word. Patron of workers and of a happy death.

Camel-hair, locusts and wild honey; baptising in the Jordan; 'Behold the Lamb of God'; beheaded by Herod for a dancing girl's request. 'Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater.'

Born in Bethlehem, raised in Nazareth, baptised in the Jordan; preached the kingdom of God in Galilee, healed, taught in parables, was crucified under Pontius Pilate and rose on the third day. The four Gospels are his story; the rest of the Bible is read in his light.

A fisherman of Bethsaida, renamed 'Rock', who walked on water and sank, confessed Christ and was called Satan, denied him three times and wept, and preached at Pentecost. Crucified in Rome, by tradition head downward.

Son of Zebedee, 'son of thunder', who leaned on Jesus' breast at supper, stood at the cross and took Mary home. Tradition credits him with the fourth Gospel, three letters and the Apocalypse on Patmos.
Freed from seven demons, she followed Jesus from Galilee, stood at the cross, and was the first to see him risen — mistaking him for the gardener until he said her name.
Keeper of the purse who sold his master for thirty pieces of silver and identified him with a kiss; hanged himself in remorse.
Prefect of Judea AD 26–36 who found no fault in Jesus, asked 'What is truth?', washed his hands, and handed him over. Named in the Creed so that the crucifixion is fixed in history.
Client king of Rome who rebuilt the Temple on a colossal scale, murdered his own sons, and — in Matthew — ordered the slaughter of the infants of Bethlehem.
One of the seven deacons, 'full of grace and fortitude', whose speech before the Sanhedrin got him stoned; a young man named Saul held the coats.

Pharisee of Tarsus, persecutor knocked to the ground on the Damascus road, tentmaker, missionary across three journeys, prisoner, shipwrecked, author of thirteen letters that shaped Christian theology. Beheaded in Rome under Nero.
A Levite of Cyprus who sold his field for the community, vouched for the converted Saul when no one trusted him, and travelled with him on the first journey.
Presided at the Council of Jerusalem and wrote, by tradition, the letter that insists faith without works is dead. Stoned in AD 62.
Half-Greek, half-Jewish, from Lystra; Paul's constant companion and delegate, and the recipient of two letters. By tradition first bishop of Ephesus.
Paul's companion, author of the third Gospel and Acts — the only Gentile writer in the New Testament, and the one who tells us most about Mary, the poor, and women.
